extracted.intended_audience: people who follow debates about science and medicine in the news
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for members of the public and news consumers on how to assess and interpret scientific and medical research reported in the media, with emphasis on understanding peer review, publication status, and the strengths/limits of single studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is it peer reviewed?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is it peer reviewed? If not, why not?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review is a system for assessing research before publication; it tells you the research has passed scrutiny of other scientists and is considered valid, significant and original. Many research claims reported in newspapers, magazines, the internet or broadcast media are not peer reviewed; ask reporters whether the research has been published in a peer-reviewed journal and, if not, why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity (research credibility, design and methodology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment on its validity – are the research results credible; are the design and methodology appropriate?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the methods are appropriate to the question, whether the design supports the conclusions, and whether results look credible. Bear in mind peer review is not a guaranteed fraud-detection system: referees may spot some wrongdoing but deliberate falsification can be missed until others try to repeat the work. Consider sample size, controls, measurement methods and reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance (importance of the finding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge the significance - is it an important finding?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the finding represents a meaningful advance or addresses an important problem. Editors and referees assess whether a paper merits attention by the field; significance should be evaluated in the context of potential impact and relevance to public health or policy where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and proper referencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine its originality - are the results new? Does the paper refer properly to work done by others?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for claims of novelty and check whether the paper situates itself within existing literature. Proper citation of prior work suggests author awareness of context; unsupported claims of novelty or poor referencing are red flags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review checks research papers for validity, significance and originality – and for clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how clearly methods, results and conclusions are presented. Poorly explained methods or ambiguous conclusions make it hard to evaluate the work and may indicate lower quality or incomplete reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context and reproducibility (not basing conclusions on one paper)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists never draw firm conclusions from just one paper or set of results. They consider the contribution it makes in the context of other work and their own experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for whether the result is supported by other studies or is part of a body of evidence pointing to the same conclusion. Single studies are weak evidence; stronger conclusions require replication and convergence across multiple studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication details and traceability
rubrics_metrics.description: The full reference to peer-reviewed papers is likely to look like this: [example references].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek full citations (authors, year, journal, volume, pages) and the journal name. Good reporting usually indicates whether research is published and where. Beware of fake-looking citations on some websites; verify the reference and journal to confirm peer-review status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication status (conference abstracts vs peer-reviewed journal articles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research papers presented at scientific conferences have often begun a process of peer review but are usually still unpublished and preliminary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat conference reports, press releases and unpublished work as preliminary. They may represent early-stage findings that have not completed peer review and should be interpreted cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal fit, scope and selectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal editors receive many more papers than they can publish, so they use a two-step selection process. First, they consider whether the paper is a ‘fit’ for their journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the journal’s focus and selectivity: some journals publish only groundbreaking work, others specialize in subfields. The fit and prestige of the journal can be informative about how the editorial team and reviewers judged the work, though journal reputation is not a perfect measure of quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of peer review (fraud detection and time constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is not a fraud detection system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize peer review's limitations: referees may detect some issues (e.g., plagiarism or obvious data misrepresentation) but deliberate falsification can escape detection. Also, peer review takes time; while electronic processes have sped it up, thorough assessment cannot always be rushed, especially for important public-health findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential resistance to maverick or unconventional ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Is ‘maverick’ science rejected through peer review? ... referees can be cautious about unusual findings; and important insights can initially be overlooked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that novel or unexpected results may face initial scepticism; this does not automatically mean they are wrong. Over time, exceptional work that is robust will usually be recognised, but initial peer review might be cautious or slow to accept unconventional claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use expert judgement rather than a simple checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessing scientific papers cannot be done in the same way as giving a car an M.O.T. or marking a maths test. New research usually has its own unique features... which require expert judgement about their validity, significance and originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid expecting a simple checklist to resolve quality; rely on expert interpretation of methods, assumptions and context. For non-experts, seek summaries from reputable sources or ask knowledgeable people rather than applying overly simplistic rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media reporting practices and cross-checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Good journalists usually indicate whether research has been published and mention the name of the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for multiple reports and longer accounts (e.g., popular science magazines or follow-up articles) to verify that media coverage accurately reflects the research. Asking reporters 'is it peer reviewed?' encourages inclusion of publication information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use external resources to verify journal peer-review status
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no definitive list of peer-reviewed journals but you can look up the names of selected peer-reviewed journals online at the science news service EurekAlert! (www.eurekalert.org/links.php?jrnl=A)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use trusted resources (journal websites, indexing services, organisations like COPE, EurekAlert!, or library databases) to check whether a journal is peer reviewed and to find further information about editorial policies and ethical standards.
